content:
After procrastinating (and still doing so to this day…) on starting my security blog, especially my main topic about my Bachelor Thesis (Evading EDRs), I’m excited to finally publish a short post about a vulnerability I discovered in October 2025.
Hopefully, this serves as motivation to start working on some posts about some creative and working ways to bypass and evade EDR solutions.
Introduction While analyzing a Cortex security incident in October 2025 at work, I stumbled across the detection “Tampering Attempt” that led me to investigate what exactly was being monitored. After experimenting with the underlying data, I discovered that it is possible to disable the Cortex XDR Agent by modifying specific environment variables used internally by the agent.
In this post, I’ll walk through the timeline (including communication with Palo Alto) and the technical details. The vulnerability itself is quite simple and does not require any sophisticated exploit or payload.
Timeline & CVE Details 23.10.2025: Submitted technical details via the official Palo Alto vulnerability disclosure form 12.12.2025: Vulnerability reproduced and confirmed 29.12.2025 – 26.01.2026: No response (to some further questions from my end) from Palo Alto despite multiple follow-ups 27.01.2026: Content Update 2120 released (fix included, but not yet communicated) 28.01.2026 – 02.03.2026: Continued lack of communication 03.03.2026 (Palo Alto): Response received, informing me about Content Update 2120 and additional agent-side hardening (high-level without any details) 08.04.2026: Advisory published by Palo Alto Vulnerability Date: April 8, 2026
Product: Cortex XDR
Affected Versions: Agent ≤ 9.0
Vendor: Palo Alto Networks
Weakness Classification: CWE-15 (External Control of System or Configuration Setting), CAPEC-578 (Disable Security Software)
Severity: Medium
CVSS: 6.7 (Base)
Advisory: https://security.paloaltonetworks.com/CVE-2026-0232
Technical Details For a long time, Cortex XDR utilises a detection called “Tampering Attempt”, designed to identify suspicious modifications to the Cortex components. One way to trigger this detection is by performing certain registry operation under: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\Cyvera\
This registry path stores a significant portion of the agent’s configuration and is a valuable source of insight for security researchers. It has also been involved in previous vulnerabilities and will likely continue to be relevant in future research regarding Cortex XDR.
Some examples of stored configuration:
Process specific monitoring via API hooks (in this example for Chrome.exe) Agent exceptions Module-level whitelisting and detection logic (in this example with DLLs excluded for Shellcode modules/detections & Mimikatz byte patterns used for its detections) Interesting Finding: Environment Variables While exploring HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\Cyvera\, I noticed two environment variables referenced in paths under “..\Cyvera\Policy\Organization\Mitigation\FileProtection\ProtectedEntries” & “..\Cyvera\PolicyTransactions{GUID}\ Organization\Mitigation\FileProtection”:
%NtTrapsProgramFiles% %NtCyveraCommonAppData% Note
Depending on the agent version or environment, these variables may differ (e.g., %trapsprogramfiles%, %cyveracommonappdata%) or are not listed at all.
These are not standard Windows environment variables (like %ProgramFiles% or %SystemRoot%), yet they are used in those keys to resolve paths to legitimate Cortex binaries.
This raised an interesting question: What happens if we control these variables?
Exploitation Direct modification of those registry values would not be feasible as modifying protected registry keys will either fail (due to missing priveleges) or trigger anti-tampering alerts. Instead, I created a system wide environment variable via PowerShell:
1 2 3 4 5 [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable( 'NtTrapsProgramFiles', 'C:\Temp', # Value does not matter, could also be empty 'Machine' ) After rebooting the system, the Cortex XDR Agent went offline permanently and was therefore not able to trigger anymore detections. Example with a LSASS Dump: Note
At the time of writing this blog post, I only had access to an older 8.5 agent; however, all newer versions up to and including 9.0 were also affected by this Vulnerability.
Unforuntately setting only a user level environment variable (which does not require administrative privileges) does not disable the agent.
Fix After applying Content Update 2120 (which should have automatically been applied in late January), any attempts to modify these environment variables will now trigger a new detection: Interestingly, the structure of the registry keys and the usage of these environment variables appear unchanged. The fix seems to rely on improved detection rather than a fundamental architectural change.
Further Experimentation Disabling Without Reboot The exploit requires a reboot because the agent only re-reads environment variables during startup. Attempts to restart the agent manually were unsuccessful:
cytool requires a password No alternative method to restart the agent was identified However, the agent does restart automatically during upgrades. This introduces a theoretical attack scenario (although rather unlikely):
Modify/Create the environment variable Wait for an agent update to be deployed The agent restarts automatically The agent comes back up in a disabled state I tested this using a VM snapshot of an old 8.5 agent:
The agent restarted automatically after approximately 10 minutes (with active internet connectivity) After the Agent Upgrade, the agent remained disabled Takeaways Vendor communication during coordinated disclosure can be slow or inconsistent The HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\Cyvera\ registry hive remains a valuable target for research. There are likely additional Detection bypasses, Evasion techniques or even Vulnerabilities just waiting to be discovered…
title: Disabling the Cortex XDR Agent (CVE-2026-0232)
